of them. However it does lie perfectly on a great circle between the B component direction and a Keweenawan normal polarity direction of about D=295 ø , I=30 ø . The latter direction corresponds to an age of about 1085 Ma on the APWP in the midst of the long normal superchron of Halls and Pesonen [1982]. This is a likely time for intrusion of the normal polarity lamprophyre dikes and the Nemegosenda carbonatite, the closest large Keweenawan complex to the C component sites. Thus the C component could be a localized hybrid of the B component and a Keweenawan normal chemical remanent magnetization (CRM), both residing in similar high coercivity and unblocking temperature spectra. Alternatively the C component could be a tilted B component because the correction of C for a 40 ø WNW tilt aligns it almost perfectly with B. This alternative requires minor local- ized block faulting along subsidiaries of the ILCZ after 1.88 Ga. Evidence for both minor later faulting and localized hydrothermal effects is seen in minor fault offsets found in the 1.1 Ga Lacknet Lake and Nemegosenda carbonatite complexes [Parsons, 1961], and in the 1.8 to 1.7 Ga and 1.2 to 1.0 Ga K/At and 40Ar/39Ar age dates found near the ILCZ [Archibald et al., 1986; Lopez Martinez and York, 1986]. Conclusions Since the NB and HSE magnetizations are characterized by both normal and reverse polarity, this suggests that primary remanences have been recorded. The well-defined and charac- teristic Matachewan remanence found in the north-northwest- trending Gamitagama diabase dikes (GD) constrains the mini- mum age of the NB and HSE magnetizations at >2.45 Ga. The results from other paleomagnetic studies of the Matachewan swarm similarly constrain the minimum age for the rest of the prefolding Archean poles in the Superior Province. The presence of both polarities, apositive contact test, precise U-Pb zircon ages, and the concordancy of the NB and HSE poles with the Archean APWP derived from other rock units in other subprovinces of the Superior Province are strong arguments in favor of our interpretation of the ages of the NB and HSE remanences

an granites and Matachewan dikes in the Michipicoten and Gamitagama greenstone belts in the western Wawa Subprovince of the Superior Province, Ontario. Detailed alternating-field and thermal step demagnetization analyses were used to isolate stable remanence directions. A single-component remanence was isolated within three adjacent dated granitic plutons on the eastern margin of the Michipicoten belt, including the Hawk Lake trondhjernite, the Southern external granite, and the Eastern external granite (HSE). The maximum possible age for this remanence is constrained by the intrusion of the last pluton at 2694 Ma. The corresponding HSE paleopole is located at low, 41"s (dp = 8", dm = 13"). A second paleopole, NB, is derived from the Northern external granite and the Baldhead River quartz monzonite, which give U-Pb zircon ages of 2662 and 2668 Ma, respectively. Further paleomagnetic sites were sampled at Wenebegon Lake, which lies 100 krn north of Rocky Island Lake (Figs. 1,4) and is also in the Abitibi Subprovince, at latitude 47"25'N, longitude 83O05'W. A number of vertical dykes, striking 350°, outcrop on the lake shore and islands, where country rocks are granitic, felsic, and mafic gneiss. On the basis of the aeromag- netic data, the dykes represent a sector of the swarm immediately to the east of those sampled at Rocky Island Lake. Petrography The Matachewan dykes are quartz tholeiites containing calcic plagioclase, pyroxene, amphibole, quartz, iron oxides, and sulphides, and their most distinguishing feature is the common occurrence of large, green, anorthositic plagioclase pheno- crysts, up to 10 cm across (Condie et aE. 1987), which are believed to have formed in shallow crustal magma chambers prior to dyke emplacement (Phinney et al. 1988). rthositic plagioclase pheno- crysts, up to 10 cm across (Condie et aE. 1987), which are believed to have formed in shallow crustal magma chambers prior to dyke emplacement (Phinney et al. 1988). Phenocrysts are common in the dykes at Rocky Island and Wenebegon lakes and appear to have accumulated on the southeast side of constrictions in apophyses at site RL7 (Fig. 5). This phenome- non may be an indicator of a component of magma flow during dyke emplacement toward the northwest, consistent with the southerly source postulated by Fahrig (1987). The dykes are green in the field, usually a sign that they have been hydrously altered. Thin sections reveal the typical suite of minerals described by Condie et al. (1987). However, plagio- clase tends to be very dusty in appearance, some samples contain patches of fine clay minerals, and chlorite (which causes the green colour) is abundant in all samples. Occasionally, skeletal opaque minerals, almost completely replaced by chlorite, can be recognized. The alteration is observed both at the margins and within the main body of the dyke. If more than one specimen was analysed from a block sample, data were combined to give a sample mean before the site mean was calculated. A secondary objective is to test the extent to which the Matachew- an and Kapuskasing dykes have been involved in KSZ tecton- ics. Our study is based on paleomagnetic data from more than 600 oriented samples collected at 68 sites from the western half of the Matachewan swarm and from the Kapuskasing dykes in the vicinity of Chapleau, along Highway 101 to the west and northwards as far as Missinaibi Lake (Fig. 2). Received January 25, 199 1 Revision accepted July 18, 1991 Mokowan Butte in southwestern Alberta is capped by 32 m of unconsolidated sediment comprising five tills and their associated paleosols. Previous stratigraphic work has indicated that the older tills are probably Early Pleistocene to late Tertiary in age. Paleomagnetic studies, based on 125 samples, show that the uppermost till-paleosol unit and the modem subsoil are normally magnetized, whereas the till-paleosol units from the middle of the sequence have reversed magnetization. We argue that these belong to the Brunhes and Matuyama polarity zones, respectively. The lowest part of the sequence has not been studied in detail and is generally too coarse for paleomagnetic sampling, and samples that have been obtained contain no accurate record of the paleofield. These new data, together with those from Wellsch Valley in Saskatchewan, Banks Island in the Northwest Temtories, Fort Selkirk in the Yukon, and Memtt in British Columbia, bring to five the number of early Quaternary sequences in Canada that have yielded a record of glacial sediments deposited during the Matuyama chron, and hence record glacial events prior to the last reversal of the geomagnetic field (720 ka). Alternating-field and thermal step demagnetization methods isolate an A remanence component with a mean direction of D = 134.6", I = 54.1" (09, = 39, k = 94, N = 19). Isothermal remanent magnetization tests confirm that this A magnetization component is preserved in pseudosingle to multidomain magnetite and in hematite. Contact tests with intruded older rocks of the Peter Lake domain, with younger crosscutting mafic dikes and with younger crosscutting shear zones, indicate that A is a primary remanence. Its pole position of 67"W, 9"N (dp = 3", dm = 5") confirms that it was formed along the margin of the Slave-Rae-Hearne craton, supporting tectonic models that it records a suture zone. The Wathaman batholith is thought to be an ensialic magmatic arc that defines the location of the northwest-dipping THO suture zone. Thus it is an obvious target for paleomagnetic study to better understand the geometry of closure of the THO. Geology The Wathaman batholith, sometimes called the Wathaman- Chipewyan batholith, in Saskatchewan and Manitoba is a megacrystic granitoid pluton that is over 900 km long and over 150 km wide in places, making it the world's largest known Precambrian pluton (Fig. 1) (Fumerton et al. 1984). This massive monzogranite-granodiorite pluton is remarkably homogeneous and shows little evidence of multiple intrusive episodes (Lewry et al. 1981). The batholith's northwestern contact is defined by blastomylonites in the major Needle Falls ' Lithoprobe Publication 243. and Parker Lake shear zones that separate it from the Wolla- ston and Seal River fold belts and the Archean Peter Lake domain. The fold belts define the deformed margin of the Archean Hearne province, outboard of which are the Rae and Slave provinces (Hoffman 1988). On the southeastern side of the Wathaman batholith is the intervening juvenile Early Proterozoic crust of the THO. This zone

parate it from the Wolla- ston and Seal River fold belts and the Archean Peter Lake domain. The fold belts define the deformed margin of the Archean Hearne province, outboard of which are the Rae and Slave provinces (Hoffman 1988). On the southeastern side of the Wathaman batholith is the intervening juvenile Early Proterozoic crust of the THO. This zone is composed of intraoceanic rocks of several domains which are relicts of the Manikewan oceanic basin and extend southeastwards to the Archean Superior province (Stauffer 1984). The Wathaman batholith is comprised of richly porphyritic quartz monzonite, grading to granodiorite and granite in this study area (Lewry et al. 1980a, 1980b; Johnston 1985). The abundance and size of the microcline megacrysts decrease near the batholith's margins. A weak primary flow foliation, acquired during magmatic emplacement, is seen in the pre- ferential alignment of the megacrysts. Superimposed on the primary fabric is the main flaser and mylonite fabric associated with the shearing and compressional event that formed the Needle Falls and Parker Lake shear zones. The Wathaman batholith is thought to be an ensialic magmatic arc that defines the location of the northwest-dipping THO suture zone. Thus it is an obvious target for paleomagnetic study to better understand the geometry of closure of the THO. Geology The Wathaman batholith, sometimes called the Wathaman- Chipewyan batholith, in Saskatchewan and Manitoba is a megacrystic granitoid pluton that is over 900 km long and over 150 km wide in places, making it the world's largest known Precambrian pluton (Fig. 1) (Fumerton et al. 1984). This massive monzogranite-granodiorite pluton is remarkably homogeneous and shows little evidence of multiple intrusive episodes (Lewry et al. 1981). The batholith's northwestern contact is defined by blastomylonites in the major Needle Falls ' Lithoprobe Publication 243. and Parker Lake shear zones that separate it from the Wolla- ston and Seal River fold belts and the Archean Peter Lake domain. The fold belts define the deformed margin of the Archean Hearne province, outboard of which are the Rae and Slave provinces (Hoffman 1988). On the southeastern side of the Wathaman batholith is the intervening juvenile Early Proterozoic crust of the THO. This zone

The fold belts define the deformed margin of the Archean Hearne province, outboard of which are the Rae and Slave provinces (Hoffman 1988). On the southeastern side of the Wathaman batholith is the intervening juvenile Early Proterozoic crust of the THO. This zone is composed of intraoceanic rocks of several domains which are relicts of the Manikewan oceanic basin and extend southeastwards to the Archean Superior province (Stauffer 1984). The Wathaman batholith is comprised of richly porphyritic quartz monzonite, grading to granodiorite and granite in this study area (Lewry et al. 1980a, 1980b; Johnston 1985). The abundance and size of the microcline megacrysts decrease near the batholith's margins. A weak primary flow foliation, acquired during magmatic emplacement, is seen in the pre- ferential alignment of the megacrysts. Superimposed on the primary fabric is the main flaser and mylonite fabric associated with the shearing and compressional event that formed the Needle Falls and Parker Lake shear zones. This change in polarity is a consequence of uplift within the KSZ, exposing deeper levels of dykes that acquired their magnetization in a younger "normal" polarity epoch (Halls and Palmer 1990; Bates and Halls 1990). These regional variations are statistically significant at the 95% confidence level, and cannot be attributed to remagnetization or to magnetic anisotropy. The magnetization of the Matachewan dykes could be deflected either as a result of intrinsic anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility of the diabase (Stacey 1960), or from shape anisotropy related to the tabular nature of dyke bodies (Abrahamsen 1986). here for the first time, reveal that the dykes contain a dual-polarity primary remanence that varies across the swarm in both inclination and declination. These regional variations are statistically significant at the 95% confidence level, and cannot be attributed to remagnetization or to magnetic anisotropy. Inclination variation is probably due to real or apparent polar wander during the emplacement of the swarm, and may in part explain the declination variation as well. However, for dykes within and northwest of the Kapuskasing Structural Zone (KSZ) a positive correlation is found between regionally averaged values of declination and dyke trend. Here the dykes appear to have suffered differential rotations about vertical axes of up to 40° since emplacement. The Matachewan swarm radiates northwards from a broad focus situated approximately in northern Lake Huron but the trend of the western half of the swarm follows a broad Z-shaped pattern where it crosses the KSZ. Our data suggest that this changing trend is a secondary feature and that the western dykes, like their eastern counterparts, originally had a more uniform trend. Magnetic anisotropy Other possible causes of paleomagnetic variation are the effects of magnetic anisotropy. The magnetization of the Matachewan dykes could be deflected either as a result of intrinsic anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility of the diabase (Stacey 1960), or from shape anisotropy related to the tabular nature of dyke bodies (Abrahamsen 1986). In the first instance, anisotropy may arise from flow patterns in the dyke such that the maximum susceptibility axis lies within the dyke plane parallel to paleoflow, and the minimum axis is perpendicular to the dyke. For essentially vertical dykes, we would expect to see a deflection in the paleomagnetic declination towards the plane of the dyke, by an amount dependent on the angle between the paleofield and dyke plane. Conclusions A characteristic high-coercivity, dual polarity, primary rem- anence has been recovered from the entire Matachewan dyke swarm. Although the signature is readily recognized as Mata- chewan, significant variations occur in both declination and inclination of the magnetization. The inclination changes are most easily explained in terms of either apparent or true wander of the geomagnetic pole, such that later dykes were intruded in a 20" steeper ambient paleofield. These regional variations are statistically significant at the 95% confidence level, and cannot be attributed to remagnetization or to magnetic anisotropy. Inclination variation is probably due to real or apparent polar wander during the emplacement of the swarm, and may in part explain the declination variation as well. The magnetization of the Matachewan dykes could be deflected either as a result of intrinsic anisotropy of magnetic susceptibility of the diabase (Stacey 1960), or from shape anisotropy related to the tabular nature of dyke bodies (Abrahamsen 1986). In the first instance, anisotropy may arise from flow patterns in the dyke such that the maximum susceptibility axis lies within the dyke plane parallel to paleoflow, and the minimum axis is perpendicular to the dyke. These regional variations are statistically significant at the 95% confidence level, and cannot be attributed to remagnetization or to magnetic anisotropy. Inclination variation is probably due to real or apparent polar wander during the emplacement of the swarm, and may in part explain the declination variation as well. Conclusions (1) RLR, the characteristic magnetization of the unaltered Red Lake batholiths, is probably a primary TRM acquired ~ 2700 Ma ago (4°Ar/ 39Ar initial cooling age [3]) and carried by both magnetite and deuteric hematite. Group 1 includes the Hammell Lake, Killala Baird, Trout Lake and Little Vermilion Lake batholiths, which were intruded between 2730 and 2700 Ma ago (U/Pb, zircon). Group 2 includes the Howey diorite, the Dome Stock, and dikes and andesites from the Dickenson mine. These units, from the mineralized deformation zones (DZs) between the batholiths, were sheared and hydrothermally altered in the same event that caused gold mineralization in supracrustal units. Previous studies Three distinct directions of paleomagnetic remanence have been reported in the literature. The dominant down-west mag- netization was described in a number of studies including Strangway (1961), Fahrig et al. (1965), Larochelle (1966), Irving and Naldrett (1977), and Schutts and Dunlop (1981). However, it is now known (e.g., Buchan et al. 1989, caption to Fig. 12; Ernst and Buchan 1993) that Abitibi dykes of Middle Proterozoic age and Biscotasing dykes of Early Pro- terozoic age were not differentiated in this early work because both swarms carry down-west remanences. A second rernanence (herein called the Senneterre remanence) has been reported in the literature at only four sites. It was recognized as an up-north magnetization by Larochelle (1966) at three sampling sites in two dykes, and as a magnetization of opposite polarity by Symons et al. (1981) at a single site. Preliminary unpublished work (W.F. Fahrig, personal com- munication 1985) indicated that this magnetization occurs in other northeast-trending quartz tholeiite ,dykes. Finally, a third shallow south-southwest remanence direc- tion was obtained by Larochelle (1966) at four sites from a single dyke. In some samples, pyroxenes are highly altered, whereas primary plagioclases are largely unaffected. In other samples, the converse is true. In yet others, all of the primary minerals are altered. Core samples were then distributed among the participating laboratories for standard palaeomagnetic measurements. A pilot collection ( 18 samples), representative of all rock types sampled, was subjected to a variety of rock-magnetic experiments at the Institute of Physics of the Earth in Moscow. These experiments include determinations of saturation magnetization J, and saturation remanence J,, as a function of temperature, as well as AF and DC demagnetization of Jrs. The peak fields used for the latter two experiments reach 100 mT and 2000 mT respectively. In addition, stepwise thermal and AF demagnetization experi- ments were carried out on specimens from the pilot cpllection. A magnetically shielded furnace (inner residual field < 15 nT) was used for the demagnetization experiments, yhereas AF demagnetization was achieved by using a two-axis tumbler system, housed in a set of Helmholtz coils in order to com- pensate for the Earth's local magnetic field in the laboratory. In the case of stronger remanence, continuous thermal demagnetization was carried out in a thermal demagnetizer incorporated in the spinner magnetometer. In addition, stepwise thermal and AF demagnetization experi- ments were carried out on specimens from the pilot cpllection. A magnetically shielded furnace (inner residual field < 15 nT) was used for the demagnetization experiments, yhereas AF demagnetization was achieved by using a two-axis tumbler system, housed in a set of Helmholtz coils in order to com- pensate for the Earth's local magnetic field in the laboratory. Thermal and alternating-field demagnetization experiments reveal the presence of several components of the natural remanent magnetization of normal and reversed polarity. Component A, has been identified in a sill of Vepsian gabbro-dolerites (1770 Ma) exposed at Rybreka locality and yields a palaeopole at 37.8"N, 210.6"E (dp = 4.0", dm = 7.7'). This magnetization is interpreted to be of thermoremanent origin. In the Vepsian Shoksha quartzite (ca. 1800 Ma) cut by the sill and in the underlying basalts, the palaeopoles indicated by the presumably primary components A, and A, are at 45.1"N, 206.4"E (dp = 3.6", dm = 6.5") and 44.2"N, 241.5"E (dp = 6.1", dm = 9.6") respectively. The thermomagnetic analysis of dolerites from the Shoksha and Sheltozero areas gave similar, but not so strongly convincing, results (Fig. 13, sample B91). 4.2.6 Burakovka area Ultramaﬁtes are found amongst the samples from the Aganozero block of the Burakovka layered intrusion. Thermomagnetic analysis of these samples gives results that are characteristic for magnesium magnetite with a small percentage of MgO, which indicates a primary origin for this magnetite. On the other hand, petrographic and microprobe investigations have established the presence of secondary olivine-generated magnetite, which appeared during serpentinization of the Aganozero peridotites (Pisakin et al. 1992). Thermomagnetic analysis of gabbro-norites yields Jrs(T ) dependences charac- teristic of virtually pure magnetite, whereas the decay curves Jn(T ) (see Fig. 8, sample B59), in conjunction with microscopic and microprobe analyses, indicate a thermoremanent origin of the NRM in the gabbro-norites. These latter rocks, which contain so-called ‘cloudy’ plagioclase, yield results that are consistent with the formation of magnetite within such plagio- clase during the consolidation of the Burakovka intrusion (Pisakin et al. 1992).

To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S,

(corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S, 304.8° E, A95=8.3° ; U–Pb age of 2436± 25 Ma), the Voche-Lambina ultramaﬁcs and amphibolites (12.9 ° N, 314.1° E, A95=8.6° ; Rb–Sr age of 2198 ± 172 Ma), and the Kolvitsa peridotites and schists (44.2° N, 232.6° E, A95=5.4° ; assigned magnetization age of 1900 Ma). For the Karelian Province, reference poles are presented for the Burakovka gabbro-norites (19.5 ° S, 262.6° E, A95=7.2° ; Sm–Nd age of 2439± 22 Ma), the Matozero doleritic dykes (20.6° S, 308.5° E, A95=12.3° ; U–Pb age of 2150 ± 60 Ma), and the Ropruchey Sill gabbro- dolerites (40.5 ° N, 229.8° E, A95=8.1° ; U–Pb age of 1770 ± 12 Ma). Although some NRM components of other rocks are not as precisely dated, a number of palaeomagnetic poles are in good internal agreement, forming two tracks of the Lower Proterozoic apparent polar wander path (APWP). A preliminary version of the pre-Svecofennian APWP tracks for the Karelian and Kola–Belomorian provinces is proposed. Our results conﬁrm the general drift pattern of Fennoscandia in the Proterozoic and support the idea of the absence of large-scale block movements within t

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 po

Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Of these, six might be classiﬁed as reference poles. For the Kola and Belomorian provinces there are poles from the Main Range gabbro-dolerites (16.7° S,

gnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Archaean and Palaeoproterozoic palaeomagnetic data from the Fennoscandian Shield were predominantly obtained from the Karelian and Svecofennian provinces. Few poles from the Lapland granulite belt of the Belomorian Province and from Kola Province were available for the Elming et al. (1993) compilation and their reconstruction of the Fennoscandian APWP. Received 1998 November 22; in original form 1997 July 22 SUMMARY The palaeomagnetic data that are available for the eastern Fennoscandian Shield are too sparse to allow any palaeomagnetic constraints to be determined for intracratonic horizontal movements in this part of the shield. To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. Palaeomagnetic data oVer the possibility of addressing some of these questions; until now, however, only the Canadian Shield has yielded enough Precambrian palaeomagnetic data to indi- cate signiﬁcant intracratonic movements (Symons 1991). As for the Fennoscandian Shield, there is as yet no palaeomagnetic evidence that can resolve that degree of movement. An apparent polar wander path (APWP) for the Fennoscandian Shield has recently been constructed for the time interval 2850–600 Ma, under the assumption that the Shield remained tectonically coherent during this time (Elming et al . 1993). There is, however, geological evidence which indicates that signiﬁcant intracratonic occurred during this time. Gorbatschev & Bogdanova (1993) provided evidence for rifting and the possible break-up of the shield between 2500 and 2000 Ma. The resultant basins were then closed due to a collisional orogeny between 1950 and 1820 Ma, possibly marking the formation of a Proterozoic supercontinent (Piper 1987). On the other hand, the Arc

To address this issue we have obtained new palaeomagnetic data from maﬁc and ultramaﬁc plutons, sills, dykes and basement country rocks in the Kola, Belomorian and Karelian provinces of the Fennoscandian Shield. A number of natural remanent magnetization (NRM) components were isolated, and we associate these with various events of Precambrian tectonomagmatic activity within the eastern Fennoscandian Shield. 36 palaeomagnetic poles were obtained. 12 poles, with ages ranging from 1700 Ma to 2450 Ma, satisfy the accepted reliability criteria (corresponding to the ‘B-category’ of Briden & DuV 1981). Its pole position at 3 °N, 52°W (dp= 7 °, dm= 12 ° ) locates the Peter Lake domain along the margin of the SRH craton at the time of metamorphism and was later rotated 32 ° + 14 ° counterclockwise, probably when the abutting southwestern arm of the Wathaman batholith was similarly rotated during oroclinal deformation. B has a direction of D= 92 °, I= 83 ° (ot9s = 8 °. k= 19, N= 20) that gives a pole at 54°N, 80 °W (dp= 15 o, dm= 15 ° ). The B remanence is thought to have been acquired at about 1780 Ma during the D3 shearing event. This event produced the Needle Falls and Parker Lake shear zones that separate the Peter Lake domain from the Wollaston fold belt and Wathaman batholith, respectively. The B component likely defines the end of the Trans-Hudson orogenic event during which the 5000 km wide Manikewan ocean closed. Thorough evaluation of the Andean collisional model for the THO will require much more paleomagnetic data. 1. Introduction

Experimental methods The Peter Lake domain was sampled at 28 sites along the Highway 105 transect and the shore- line of Peter Lake (Fig. 2). Of these sites, twenty are in the metagabbros and three in the monzon- ites of the Peter Lake complex. The remaining five sites are in the Parker Lake mafic gneisses to provide paleomagnetic contact tests between the Wathaman batholith and the Peter Lake do- main, and between the gneisses and the complex in the domain. Five cores were drilled at most sites and ori- ented in situ by sun compass. Two specimens were later sliced from most cores to yield a total collection of 259 specimens. All measurements were done inside a shielded room. The speci- mens' natural remanent magnetizations (NRM) were measured using an automated CTF DRM- 420 cryogenic magnetometer. One specimen from each site was alternating field (AF) demag- netized in twelve steps to 120 mT using a Sap- phire Instruments SI-4 demagnetizer, and a sec- ond specimen

The Par- ker Lake B component is also statistically iden- tical to the Wathaman batholith's C component at 64°N, 105°W (dp=33 °, dm=34 °) which is found in sheared granite sites (Symons, 1991 ), especially in the four sites from immediately south of the batholith's contact with the gneisses on the HW 105 transect. Combining the data from the fourteen B component sites of this study with the six equivalent C sites from the Watha- man study gives an overall pole at 54°N, 80°W (dp= 15 °, dm= 15 ° ). This pole falls on the 1650 Ma position of the Irving ( 1979 ) apparent polar wander path (APWP). This age is certainly too young because the D3 event must have preceded the onset of deposition of the undeformed Atha- baska sandstones at about 1735+15 Ma that conformably overly the Wathaman batholith about 35 km west of site 22 (Lewry et al., 1980; Hoffman, 1989; Machado, 1990). It is possible that the B component in the shear zones was af- fected by retrograde metamorphism in the later D4 or final D5 deformation events. Some evi- dence that the B magnetization component is more complex and, perhaps, represents more than one event is seen in Fig. 3b. Summary The metamorphosed gabbro-monzonite rock suite of the Peter Lake complex retains a com- mon A ChRM direction in magnetic domains with unblocking temperatures ranging from about 300 to 700°C. The A component predates intrusion of the adjacent massive 1854+ 11 Ma Wathaman batholith, and correlates most evi- dently with the D 1 regional metamorphic event in the Peter Lake domain. The best estimate for the age of the D 1 event and of the A component is 1869 + 29 Ma based on scant radiometric data, but it is unlikely to be older than the onset of the Hudsonian orogeny at about 1900 Ma. ons in time and space during closure. 2. Geology The Peter Lake domain is a northeasterly- trending cigar-shaped terrane about 200 km in length and 50 km in width. It is separated on its northwestern side from the Wollaston fold belt of the SRH craton by the Needle Falls shear zone, and on its southeastern side from the Wathaman batholith by the Parker Lake shear zone. Both zones are en P.chelon ductile mylonitic shears with dextral strike-slip displacements (LewD, and Collerson, 1990). The domain is comprised of medium- to coarse-grained plutonic rocks of dioritic to gabbroic composition with minor me- tapyroxenite and anorthosite that have been in- truded by granitic rocks ranging from monzonite to alaskite in composition (Lewry et al., 1980). In the study area (Fig. 2), the mafic rocks are mostly weakly foliated gabbros, metagabbros and amphibolites, and the granitic rocks are quartz- bearing monzonites to biotite monzogranite. These units were metamorphosed in the regional D 1 deformational event, D2 was a minor local- ized event that preceded emplacement of the Wathaman batholith. cedure The Tsuomasvarri intrusions form a well-ex- posed 435 m high hill. Fifty-five oriented core samples were taken from ten sites in the ultra- marie intrusion (Fig. 3), using the techniques described previously in Mertanen et al. ( 1987 ). The majority of the samples (45) are olivine py- roxenites, six are serpentinite dunites and four are hornblendites (see Fig. 3). In the surround- ing gabbro-diorite 46 samples were taken from ten sites (Fig. 3 ). The NRM was measured on spinner magne- tometers (Pesonen et al., 1983). AF demagneti- zations were done with a single-axis demagne- tizer (in steps of 10 mT, up to 100 mT), and thermal demagnetization was performed (in steps of 100°C up to 500°C and then in 20-10°C steps up to 680 °C ) in Schonstedt or homemade furnaces (Leino, 1979; Pesonen et al., 1983). Pesonen Laboratory for Palaeomagnetism, Geological Survey of Finland, SF-02150 Espoo, Finland Received June 22, 1992; revised version accepted January 27, 1994 Abstract Preliminary palaeomagnetic results are presented for the Proterozoic Tsuomasvarri central ultramafic intrusion and surrounding, older gabbro-diorite intrusion in the northeastern Fennoscandian shield. In the ultramafic intru- sion, five remanence components, reflecting different geological processes, were isolated in the alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization of 55 samples from ten sites. A reversed polarity remanence component C (pole: Plat = 26 °N, Plon = 245 ° E, dp= 5 °, dm = 9 °, n = 32 samples) dominates in the ultramafic intrusion. The normal polarity pole A (Plat=44°N, Plon=232°E, dp=4 °, din=6 °, n=9 samples) corresponds to an age of ~ 1.88 Ga on the Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP), and is probably a thermochemical remanence acquired during the Svecokarelian orogeny or in the late stages of magma cooling. Pole B (Plat = 35 ° N, Plon = 158 ° E, dp = 9 °, dm = 15 °, n = 5 samples, normal polarity) corresponds to the ~ 1.75 Ga old post-orogenic activity in the area, and is also seen

cedure The Tsuomasvarri intrusions form a well-ex- posed 435 m high hill. Fifty-five oriented core samples were taken from ten sites in the ultra- marie intrusion (Fig. 3), using the techniques described previously in Mertanen et al. ( 1987 ). The majority of the samples (45) are olivine py- roxenites, six are serpentinite dunites and four are hornblendites (see Fig. 3). In the surround- ing gabbro-diorite 46 samples were taken from ten sites (Fig. 3 ). The NRM was measured on spinner magne- tometers (Pesonen et al., 1983). AF demagneti- zations were done with a single-axis demagne- tizer (in steps of 10 mT, up to 100 mT), and thermal demagnetization was performed (in steps of 100°C up to 500°C and then in 20-10°C steps up to 680 °C ) in Schonstedt or homemade furnaces (Leino, 1979; Pesonen et al., 1983). Susceptibilities were measured in the course of thermal demagnetizations (in steps of 200°C, 300°C, 400°C, 500°C, 520°C, 570°C, 600°C, 640°C and 680°C) to detect mineralogical changes, interpreted on the basis of changes in bulk susceptibility during heating. Magnetiza- tions were isolated using principal component analyses (Kirschvink, 1980) with maximum an- gular deviation (MAD) values of 6 ° in most samples and up to 10 ° in some cases with larger scatter. Probably due to the dif- fering abilities of the rocks to resist remagneti- zations, some magnetizations are encountered only sporadically throughout the various sites. Usually one specimen carries one or two differ- ent components and the components vary from specimen to specimen. In addition, most sam- ples reveal a large component of the present Earth's field (PEF) magnetization which also diminishes the number of accepted samples. For this reason the number of samples used in the analysis is unfortunately fairly low for obtaining statistically well defned means. However, we re- port the results of these investigations, knowing that the interpretations are based on limited data. For the Tsuomasvarri ultramafic intrusion, we have separated five remanence components (hereafter called A, B, C, D and F) all of which we believe to have geological significance. The ultramafic intrusion is dominated by a well- grouped southeasterly and moderate upward magnetization, C. Based on varying compositions within the intrusion, Kesola (1992) has suggested that the gabbro-diorite was formed through ultrametamorphism and remo- bilization of the originally Archaean gneisses. Vaasjoki, in Forsberg- Heikkil~i, 1989) showed that the gabbro-diorite is as young as of Svecokarelian age (1.93 Ga) and since it cuts the ultramafic intrusion, the ul- tramafic intrusion is younger than 1.93 Ga. Fur- thermore, samples from the Isokivennokka gran- ite did not give reliable palaeomagnetic results. Hence, plate tectonic interpretations of the Kola suture belt could not be tested with palaeomag- netic data. Palaeomagnetic investigations were carded out on the Tsuomasvard layered ultramafic intru- sion and the surrounding gabbro-diorite intru- sion (Fig. 3 ), because they proved to carry mul- ticomponent remanent magnetizations (Mertanen and Pesonen, 1992 ). It is important to isolate the different magnetizations, because they can have been formed in several thermal, chemical or hydrothermal processes and may thus reflect the complex geological evolution of the northern Fennoscandian shield. The aim of this paper is to study the nature and origin of these magnetizations. We have attempted to as- sociate the magnetizations with geologic events in the northern Fennoscandian shield by dating them, using isotopic age determinations and by comparing pole positions with poles of previous studies from Fennoscandia. 2. Pesonen Laboratory for Palaeomagnetism, Geological Survey of Finland, SF-02150 Espoo, Finland Received June 22, 1992; revised version accepted January 27, 1994 Abstract Preliminary palaeomagnetic results are presented for the Proterozoic Tsuomasvarri central ultramafic intrusion and surrounding, older gabbro-diorite intrusion in the northeastern Fennoscandian shield. In the ultramafic intru- sion, five remanence components, reflecting different geological processes, were isolated in the alternating field (AF) and thermal demagnetization of 55 samples from ten sites. A reversed polarity remanence component C (pole: Plat = 26 °N, Plon = 245 ° E, dp= 5 °, dm = 9 °, n = 32 samples) dominates in the ultramafic intrusion. The normal polarity pole A (Plat=44°N, Plon=232°E, dp=4 °, din=6 °, n=9 samples) corresponds to an age of ~ 1.88 Ga on the Apparent Polar Wander Path (APWP), and is probably a thermochemical remanence acquired during the Svecokarelian orogeny or in the late stages of magma cooling. vity in the area, and is also seen in results of K-Ar (whole rock) isotopic age determinations from the vicinity. The normal polarity pole D (pole: Plat = 25 ° S, Plon = 285 ° E, dp = 12 °, dm = 19 °, n = 11 samples) has a palaeomagnetic age of ~ 2.44 Ga which is in contrast with the isotopic age determination of 1.93 Ga (U-Pb age on zircon) of the gabbro-diorite intrusion. Pole F (Plat = 3 ° N, Plon = 212 ° E, dp = 10 °, dm = 18 °, n = 5 samples ) indicates an age of 0.5-0.4 Ga on the Palaeozoic APWP segment of Fennoscandia and probably reflects a weak Caledonian overprint in northeastern Finland. In the gabbro-diorite intrusion, two remanence components were isolated in 46 samples from eight sites. The palaeomagnetic age, ~ 1.93 Ga, of the dominant normal polarity component, A' (pole: Plat = 40 ° N, Plon = 247 ° E, dp= 5 °, dm= 8 °, n= 28 samples) is consistent with the isotopic age of 1.93 Ga (U-Pb determination on zircon). The normal polarity component D (pole: Plat=20°S, Plon=285°E, dp= 14 °, dm=23 °, n---5 samples), which was also isolated in the ultramafic intrusion, contradicts the U-Pb isotopic age determination. 1. Introduction In the last decade the northeastern Fennoscan- dian shield has been a subject of keen interest among those seeking to understand the forma

ic study. On geological grounds it was suggested that the Tsuomasvarri ultramafic in- trusion was Palaeoproterozoic in age ( ~ 2.4 Ga) (R. Kesola, pers. commun., 1986). The Ar- chaean Isokivennokka granite ( ~ 2.6 Ga) (Fig. 2 ) was chosen to represent the northeastern side of the Kola suture. Later, however, new isotopic age determinations (M. Vaasjoki, in Forsberg- Heikkil~i, 1989) showed that the gabbro-diorite is as young as of Svecokarelian age (1.93 Ga) and since it cuts the ultramafic intrusion, the ul- tramafic intrusion is younger than 1.93 Ga. Fur- thermore, samples from the Isokivennokka gran- ite did not give reliable palaeomagnetic results. Hence, plate tectonic interpretations of the Kola suture belt could not be tested with palaeomag- netic data. Palaeomagnetic investigations were carded out on the Tsuomasvard layered ultramafic intru- sion and the surrounding gabbro-diorite intru- sion (Fig. 3 ), because they proved to carry mul- ticomponent remanent magnetizations (Mertanen and Pesonen, 1992 ). It is important to isolate the different magnetizations, because they can have been formed in several thermal, chemical or hydrothermal processes and may thus reflect the complex geological evolution of the northern Fennoscandian shield. Little Bldg., Ann Arbor, M! 48109-1063, USA bUniversity of Nairobi, Nairobi, Kenya Received December, 1991; revised version accepted August, 1992 Abstract The Nyanzian System lavas of western Kenya are believed to be the oldest rocks of the Tanzanian Craton. Intrusive age relationships suggest an age >12850 Ma although direct attempts at dating the Nyanzian have pro- duced disparate results. Our study involves a suite of samples collected from the Nyanzian basalts, pillow basalts, andesites and rhyolites from sixteen sites in western Kenya. These rocks yield a tilt-corrected paleomagnetic pole at 14 o N, 150 °E (K= 59, dp = 5 °, dm = 7 ° ). This pole is constrained to be older than the first (D 1

arly defined because only a single Rb-Sr whole-rock age of 2573 +_ 34 Ma (Wendt et al., 1972) on an orthogneiss is available. Cahen et al. (1984) considered this age to represent a younger limit to the Dodoman metamorphism. The Nyanzian System consists of a succession composed of, from top to bottom: a greywacke and andesitic volcanic group with abundant banded iron formations; an intermediate group composed of rhyolites with intercalated tufts and agglomerates and a basal unit composed of marie volcanic rocks (pillow lavas and flows) with some (rare)banded ironstones (Shackleton, 1946). The total thickness of the Nyanzian Sys- tem has been estimated at 7500 m (Grantham, 1945). The Kavirondian System unconformably ov- erlies the Nyanzian rocks and is composed of pelitic rocks, arkoses and conglomerates. Nei- ther the Kavirondian nor the Nyanzian Systems are well-dated; in fact, the published ages for the Nyanzian rocks were reported by Yanagi and Suwa (1981) as 2710+340 Ma (Rb-Sr whole rock) and 2380 + 250 Ma (Rb-Sr, Bell and Dod- son, 1981 ). These ages only roughly overlap and the large errors associated with the ages suggest that neither can be considered reliable. directional_or_weak_substitution_warning.excerpt: ed August, 1992 Abstract The Nyanzian System lavas of western Kenya are believed to be the oldest rocks of the Tanzanian Craton. Intrusive age relationships suggest an age >12850 Ma although direct attempts at dating the Nyanzian have pro- duced disparate results. Our study involves a suite of samples collected from the Nyanzian basalts, pillow basalts, andesites and rhyolites from sixteen sites in western Kenya. These rocks yield a tilt-corrected paleomagnetic pole at 14 o N, 150 °E (K= 59, dp = 5 °, dm = 7 ° ). This pole is constrained to be older than the first (D 1 ) deformation ( > 2472 + 30 Ma) by positive fold, conglomerate and reversal tests. Analysis of the paleomagnetic data base for three African cratonic nuclei (Tanzanian, Kaapvaal/Zimbabwe and West Africa) for the time period from 2.0 Ga to 3.0 Ga demonstrates a paucity of well-dated poles, although there are several poles from the Kaapvaal/Zim- babwe and Tanzanian Cratons which allow "spot-readings" of their relative positions. We demonstrate, based on these data, that the Kaapvaal/Zimbabwe and Tanzanian Cratons were drifting independently at ~ 2875 Ma, ~ 2700 Ma and ~ 2450 Ma. This independent motion of the Tanzanian and Kaapvaal/Zimbabwe Cratons indicates that previously proposed models involving African cratonic

e Kaapvaal/Zimbabwe and Tanzanian Cratons were drifting independently at ~ 2875 Ma, ~ 2700 Ma and ~ 2450 Ma. This independent motion of the Tanzanian and Kaapvaal/Zimbabwe Cratons indicates that previously proposed models involving African cratonic coherence can no longer be considered valid for the time period from 2850 to 2500 Ma. The nature and style of tectonism during the Earth's infancy may one day be elucidated by a set of high-quality paleomag- netic data. In addi- tion, questions regarding the exact nature of the Earth's early magnetic field may be revealed through paleomagnetic investigations (e.g. na- ture of reversals). The BIFs are remarkable in that they can be cor- related practically across the whole basin, cov- ering an area of about 100,000 km 2. In one of the BIF units, the Dales Gorge Member, even small- scale (few centimetres) banding can be corre- lated basin-wide (Trendall and Blockley, 1970; Ewers and Morris, 1981 ). The iron ores of the Hamersley Basin are of many types and ages and have been derived, either directly or indirectly, from the BIFs. The youngest ores are the haematite conglomerates ("canga") and the pisolitic goethitic-haematitic ores, which are of late Mesozoic and Tertiary or- igin. Much older, however, are the giant micro- platy haematite BIF-hosted iron ores. These rep- resent the largest and most mature ores in the province and have been studied by many work- ers, as summarized by Morris (1983, 1985), Blockley (1990) and Harmsworth et al. ( 1990 ). The myriad of mineralogical and textural va- rieties present in the ores has been studied in de- tail by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ). Anisotropy also causes cones of confidence to be underestimated, due to compression of the range of inclinations. In principle, deflection of post-folding remanence towards the bedding plane by high magnetic anisotropy can produce an ap- parent syn-folding signature, with best agreement between directions from different fold limbs after partial unfold- ing. Thus high anisotropy cannot only bias estimated palaeofield directions and cause underestimation of errors, but can also mislead interpretation of the time of remanence acquisition. The anisotropy of anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) probably yields an upper limit to the anisotropy of the chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) carried by the BIFs. Therefore, from the anisotropy of ARM, a maximum inclination deflection of 9 ° is suggested for the sampled BIFs. This corresponds to less than 5 ° change of palaeolatitude. The palaeomagnetic pole position calculated for BIFs at Paraburdoo is 40.9 ° S, 225.0 °E (dp = 2.9 °, drn = 5.8 ° ) after tilt correction, but without correction for anisotropy. The Hamersley and Fortescue Groups were subjected to low-grade (lowermost prehnite- pumpellyite facies to lowermost greenschist fa- cies) metamorphism due to burial beneath >t 5 km of the Turee Creek Group (Smith et al., 1982), before the initial folding, uplift and par- tial erosion of the Mount Bruce Supergroup. Metamorphic temperatures in the Hamersley Group nowhere exceeded ~ 300 °C and are often considerably lower. A slightly lower grade of bur- ial metamorphism at Paraburdoo is associated with relict primary haematite overgrown by magnetite in the BIFs, whereas elsewhere, e.g. at Mount Tom Price and Wittenoom, the meta- morphic grade is higher and replacement of pri- mary haematite by magnetite is essentially com- plete (Morris, 1985 ). This is evidence that most of the magnetite in the BIFs was produced dur- ing the burial metamorphism. Klein ( 1983 ) has discussed diagenesis and metamorphism of BIF, including the generation of magnetite as a late diagenetic/low-grade metamorphic mineral. The BIFs are remarkable in that they can be cor- related practically across the whole basin, cov- ering an area of about 100,000 km 2. In one of the BIF units, the Dales Gorge Member, even small- scale (few centimetres) banding can be corre- lated basin-wide (Trendall and Blockley, 1970; Ewers and Morris, 1981 ). The iron ores of the Hamersley Basin are of many types and ages and have been derived, either directly or indirectly, from the BIFs. The youngest ores are the haematite conglomerates ("canga") and the pisolitic goethitic-haematitic ores, which are of late Mesozoic and Tertiary or- igin. Much older, however, are the giant micro- platy haematite BIF-hosted iron ores. These rep- resent the largest and most mature ores in the province and have been studied by many work- ers, as summarized by Morris (1983, 1985), Blockley (1990) and Harmsworth et al. ( 1990 ). The myriad of mineralogical and textural va- rieties present in the ores has been studied in de- tail by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ). Dales Gorge Member and the Joffre Member), the Weeli Wolli Formation and the Boolgeeda Iron Formation. The Wittenoom Dolomite occurs between the lowest two BIFs. The BIFs are remarkable in that they can be cor- related practically across the whole basin, cov- ering an area of about 100,000 km 2. In one of the BIF units, the Dales Gorge Member, even small- scale (few centimetres) banding can be corre- lated basin-wide (Trendall and Blockley, 1970; Ewers and Morris, 1981 ). The iron ores of the Hamersley Basin are of many types and ages and have been derived, either directly or indirectly, from the BIFs. The youngest ores are the haematite conglomerates ("canga") and the pisolitic goethitic-haematitic ores, which are of late Mesozoic and Tertiary or- igin. Much older, however, are the giant micro- platy haematite BIF-hosted iron ores. These rep- resent the largest and most mature ores in the province and have been studied by many work- ers, as summarized by Morris (1983, 1985), Blockley (1990) and Harmsworth et al. ( 1990 ). The myriad of mineralogical and textural va- rieties present in the ores has been studied in de- tail by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ). The Hamersley and Fortescue Groups were subjected to low-grade (lowermost prehnite- pumpellyite facies to lowermost greenschist fa- cies) metamorphism due to burial beneath >t 5 km of the Turee Creek Group (Smith et al., 1982), before the initial folding, uplift and par- tial erosion of the Mount Bruce Supergroup. Metamorphic temperatures in the Hamersley Group nowhere exceeded ~ 300 °C and are often considerably lower. A slightly lower grade of bur- ial metamorphism at Paraburdoo is associated with relict primary haematite overgrown by magnetite in the BIFs, whereas elsewhere, e.g. at Mount Tom Price and Wittenoom, the meta- morphic grade is higher and replacement of pri- mary haematite by magnetite is essentially com- plete (Morris, 1985 ). This is evidence that most of the magnetite in the BIFs was produced dur- ing the burial metamorphism. A knowledge of the remanent magnetization, the magnetic suscepti- bility and the anisotropy of magnetic suscepti- bility (AMS) of banded-iron formations (BIFs) and iron ores of the Hamersley Group was re- quired to assist in exploration. Previous palaeomagnetic work on the iron ores has been conducted by Porath and Chamalaun (1968), who showed that the ores probably formed in the Precambrian on the basis of their directions of remanent magnetizations, which were distinct from all known younger directions. Dales Gorge Member and the Joffre Member), the Weeli Wolli Formation and the Boolgeeda Iron Formation. The Wittenoom Dolomite occurs between the lowest two BIFs. The BIFs are remarkable in that they can be cor- related practically across the whole basin, cov- ering an area of about 100,000 km 2. In one of the BIF units, the Dales Gorge Member, even small- scale (few centimetres) banding can be corre- lated basin-wide (Trendall and Blockley, 1970; Ewers and Morris, 1981 ). The iron ores of the Hamersley Basin are of many types and ages and have been derived, either directly or indirectly, from the BIFs. The youngest ores are the haematite conglomerates ("canga") and the pisolitic goethitic-haematitic ores, which are of late Mesozoic and Tertiary or- igin. Much older, however, are the giant micro- platy haematite BIF-hosted iron ores. These rep- resent the largest and most mature ores in the province and have been studied by many work- ers, as summarized by Morris (1983, 1985), Blockley (1990) and Harmsworth et al. ( 1990 ). The myriad of mineralogical and textural va- rieties present in the ores has been studied in de- tail by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ). The following brief summary of current ideas on the BIF to ore transformation is far from comprehensive and only serves to give the reader a flavour of the complex evolution recognized by Morris. Fol- lowing exposure of fresh BIF during a period of uplift and erosion, iron has been concentrated at depth by an electrochemical supergene process. This involved concentration by leaching of some gangue without replacement, as well as the me- tasomatic replacement of gangue (chert and car- bonates) by hydrous iron oxides, mostly goe- thite. Magnetite in the fresh BIF is converted to martite and cation-deficient magnetite, termed "kenomagnetite" by Morris ( 1980, 1985 ), during the ore-forming process. Anisotropy also causes cones of confidence to be underestimated, due to compression of the range of inclinations. In principle, deflection of post-folding remanence towards the bedding plane by high magnetic anisotropy can produce an ap- parent syn-folding signature, with best agreement between directions from different fold limbs after partial unfold- ing. Thus high anisotropy cannot only bias estimated palaeofield directions and cause underestimation of errors, but can also mislead interpretation of the time of remanence acquisition. The anisotropy of anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) probably yields an upper limit to the anisotropy of the chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) carried by the BIFs. Therefore, from the anisotropy of ARM, a maximum inclination deflection of 9 ° is suggested for the sampled BIFs. This corresponds to less than 5 ° change of palaeolatitude. The palaeomagnetic pole position calculated for BIFs at Paraburdoo is 40.9 ° S, 225.0 °E (dp = 2.9 °, drn = 5.8 ° ) after tilt correction, but without correction for anisotropy. Other pole positions reported include that from fiat- lying BIFs from Wittenoom at 36.4 ° S, 218.9 ° E (dp = 4.6 °, dm= 9.1 ° ), from Mount Tom Price iron ore at 37.4 ° S, 220.3°E (dp= 5.7 °, din= 11.3 ° ) and from Paraburdoo ore at 36.4 ° S, 209.9°E (dp= 4.7 °, din= 8.8 ° ). The Hamersley and Fortescue Groups were subjected to low-grade (lowermost prehnite- pumpellyite facies to lowermost greenschist fa- cies) metamorphism due to burial beneath >t 5 km of the Turee Creek Group (Smith et al., 1982), before the initial folding, uplift and par- tial erosion of the Mount Bruce Supergroup. Metamorphic temperatures in the Hamersley Group nowhere exceeded ~ 300 °C and are often considerably lower. A slightly lower grade of bur- ial metamorphism at Paraburdoo is associated with relict primary haematite overgrown by magnetite in the BIFs, whereas elsewhere, e.g. at Mount Tom Price and Wittenoom, the meta- morphic grade is higher and replacement of pri- mary haematite by magnetite is essentially com- plete (Morris, 1985 ). This is evidence that most of the magnetite in the BIFs was produced dur- ing the burial metamorphism. Klein ( 1983 ) has discussed diagenesis and metamorphism of BIF, including the generation of magnetite as a late diagenetic/low-grade metamorphic mineral. It has been suggested that the change from the "anoxic" conditions conducive to BIF forma- tion, to those favouring supergene iron enrich- ment, was related to the oxygen content of the Precambrian atmosphere reaching a threshold level able to satisfy the various oxygen "sinks" (Cloud, 1983 ). section_candidates.excerpt: alaeolatitudes, but can lead to large errors in calculated palaeopoles for intermediate to moderately steep palaeolatitudes. Anisotropy also causes cones of confidence to be underestimated, due to compression of the range of inclinations. In principle, deflection of post-folding remanence towards the bedding plane by high magnetic anisotropy can produce an ap- parent syn-folding signature, with best agreement between directions from different fold limbs after partial unfold- ing. Thus high anisotropy cannot only bias estimated palaeofield directions and cause underestimation of errors, but can also mislead interpretation of the time of remanence acquisition. The anisotropy of anhysteretic remanent magnetization (ARM) probably yields an upper limit to the anisotropy of the chemical remanent magnetization (CRM) carried by the BIFs. Therefore, from the anisotropy of ARM, a maximum inclination deflection of 9 ° is suggested for the sampled BIFs. This corresponds to less than 5 ° change of palaeolatitude. The palaeomagnetic pole position calculated for BIFs at Paraburdoo is 40.9 ° S, 225.0 °E (dp = 2.9 °, drn = 5.8 ° ) after tilt correction, but without correction for anisotropy. Other pole positions reported include that from fiat- lying BIFs from Wittenoom at 36.4 ° S, 218.9 ° E

Indian Peninsular shield is trellised by several generations of dolerite dikes, particularly in the granite-greenstone terrains (see Halls, 1982). Because they are so amenable to paleo- magnetic study, they are the source of the vast majority of Precambrian paleomagnetic data from India, especially from the Dharwar craton (Naqvi et al., 1974). Unfortunately, dolerite is difficult to date radiometrically, leaving the age of most Precambrian paleo-poles from India es- sentially unknown (Hargraves and Bhalla, 1983). Sampling and laboratory procedure Five sites in each of the alkaline and dolerite swarms plus two sites in metadolerites were sam- pled for paleomagnetic study by Hargraves in 1981. Six samples (blocks or cores drilled in the field) were gathered at each of the twelve sites, and oriented with sun and magnetic compasses. Introduction The Indian Peninsular shield is trellised by several generations of dolerite dikes, particularly in the granite-greenstone terrains (see Halls, 1982). Because they are so amenable to paleo- magnetic study, they are the source of the vast majority of Precambrian paleomagnetic data from India, especially from the Dharwar craton (Naqvi et al., 1974). Sampling and laboratory procedure Five sites in each of the alkaline and dolerite swarms plus two sites in metadolerites were sam- pled for paleomagnetic study by Hargraves in 1981. Six samples (blocks or cores drilled in the field) were gathered at each of the twelve sites, and oriented with sun and magnetic compasses. NRM measurements were made with a Schon- stedt DSM-1 spinner magnetometer interfaced to an Apple IIe computer. Specimens were ther- mally demagnetized with a Schonstedt TSD-1 apparatus. The AF demagnetization equipment (maximum field 120 roT) rotates specimens around two perpendicular axes in an ambient DC field of less than 20 nT. All this equipment is housed in a magnetically shielded room. Demagnetization data were analyzed using Zijderveld vector diagrams (Dunlop, 1979) with linear regression (Kirschvink, 1980) and using the converging remagnetization circles tech- nique of Halls (1978). Pauls Department of Geology, University of Pretoria, Pretoria 0002, South Africa Received June 7, 1992; revised version accepted January 27, 1994 Abstract Palaeomagnetic data have been acquired from seventeen sampling sites in the northern Bushveld Complex, Transvaal, South Africa. Twelve sites are situated in the main zone in the Potgietersrus area, while the remaining five are in the upper zone in the Villa Nora area. Specimens were subjected to alternating field and thermal de- magnetization. Two mean directions were found. One direction represents the main z

r 100 km in length (Gain and Mostert, 1982) (Fig. 1 ). It is roughly trian- gular in outline and consists of a central felsic portion with an outer rim of basic to ultramafic rocks. Younger sedimentary cover obscures one side of the triangle and much of the centre. This limb is truncated in the south by the northeast- trending Zebedela fault that brings Karoo sedi- ments into juxtaposition with the layered mafic rocks. Quaternary and Waterberg sedimentary rocks overlay the Potgietersrus limb to the north. To the west of the limb, the roof rocks are ex- posed, and consist of a variety of acid rocks and metasediments. The Archaean granites which compose the floor are exposed to the east. The apparent polar wander path indicates a sequential emplacement process for the Bushveld Complex, starting with the intrusion of the critical zone and ending with the emplacement of the upper zone. The saturation and unblocking curves show that one to three phases of magnetic carriers are present in the samples: (1) a high coercivity (>1.2T) and high unblocking temperature (650 "C) phase corresponding to haematite; (2) a high coercivity and very low unblocking temperature (150 "C) phase (goethite); (3) low coercivity (<350 mT) and unblocking temperatures around 450 "C and 560 "C phases (titanomagnetites and magnetite); (4) an unblocking temperature around 350 "C corresponding to maghemite. Most of the curves reveal that titanomagnetites and magnetite are the predominant magnetic carriers. Microscopic observations Microscopic observations confirm this conclusion and indicate that pyrite, which sometimes seems a secondary mineral, is abundant in some samples and absent in others. It appears that there is a relationship between the presence of this mineral and the B magnetization as pyrite is absent in samples which contain only the C magnetization. After these different rock magnetism experiments, including unblocking temperatures, it can therefore be concluded that the B component of magnetization is carried essentially by titanomagnetites and the C component by magnetite. GEOLOGICAL CONTEXT The volcanics of Sidi-Said-Maschou, located about 50 km east of El Jadida (Fig. l), were first described by Gigout (1956). These rocks crop out in the valley of Oum-er-Rbia River, north of Sidi-Said-Makhou (especially at the base of Sidi-Moul-Nker) and in some tributary valleys (particularly near K. Sbal). The volcanic rocks are included in a shaly-silty succession with green shales overlain by purple shales with trilobite-bearing pink limestones levels. Purple shales and siltstones are in close relation with lava flows and sills: they appear with the first lava flows and their last occurrence slightly precedes the end of the volcanic activity. The whole succession is cut by vertical dykes. Gigout (1956) described a section with dykes, sills and lava flows at the base of Sidi-Moul-Nker. Secondary pyrrhotite is. the dominant remanence carrier in the uppermost formations of the Pechenga Group. Palaeomagnetic poles from the Kuetsyarvi Formation differ somewhat or partially overlap with coeval palaeomagnetic poles from other tectonomagmatic provinces in northern Fennoscandia, but it is premature at this stage to speculate on intraplate movements during the Early Proterozoic. section_candidates.excerpt: nts. The Budva Zone (Krasta-Cukali in Albania) crops out only in the southern Dinarides. It disappears about 20 km south of Dubrovnik where the Karst directly overthrusts the Dalmate zone (Figure 1). The sedimentary sequence of the Budva Zone remained entirely pelagic from Trias to upper Cretaceous. It became detritic during the uppermost Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) up to the Eocene when the flysch started to fill the preexisting basins. The Dalmate Zone (Kruja Zone in Albania) crops out in a narrow band all along the Adriatic coast and in all the eastern Adriatic islands (Figure 1). The Mesozoic sequence is entirely made of shelf limestones, very similar to the ones that outcrop in the Karst. For this reason the boundary between the Karst Zone and the Dalmate Zone is not clear in central and northern Dinarides. The calcareous sedimentation extends in the Dalmate Zone up to middle Eocene and is followed by middle- upper Eocene flysch. At the Eocene-Oligocene boundary the deformation reached the Dalmate Zone, which was divided in several tectonic units overthrusted onto the Adriatic foreland. Site SP12, which is geographically close to the others, belongs to the Karst Zone (Figure 2a). Four Miocene calcareous sites were sampled in continental calcarenites from the Karst Zone, near Mostar (Figure 2b). These limestones form small patches which unconformably cover older marine series and seal middle Eocene thrust faults. In the same region we also sampled one site (SP31) in the upper Miocene-Pliocene lacustrine clays of the Gacko basin, about 60 km SE of Mostar (Figure 1). This small basin, discordant on Mesozoic limestones, contains a presently exploited coal lens. Farther south, the flysch sections of the Sutorina valley monocline, which extends from Kotor to Dubrovnik, were also sampled (sites SP35, SP40, and SP41 in Figure 3). In this monocline, which follows the regional Dinaric direction, five sites (SP32, SP33, SP34, SP36, and SP37) were sampled in lagunal and marine limestones which conformably underlie the flysch. The ages of these sediments range from early to late Eocene [Cadet, 1978]. the Karst during middle Eocene. During this major event, the rigid calcareous shelf of the Karst Zone split into several tectonic slices which were thrusted southeastward onto the more external zones. After complete emersion during the Eocene, several subsident basins developed in the Karst unit and were filled by Oligocene to Pleistocene lacustrine sediments. The Budva Zone (Krasta-Cukali in Albania) crops out only in the southern Dinarides. It disappears about 20 km south of Dubrovnik where the Karst directly overthrusts the Dalmate zone (Figure 1). This result contrasts with the very coherent post-Eocene 45 ø clockwise rotation previously observed in the external Albano-Hellenides from Peloponesus to the Tirana basin. These new results suggest that the Scutari-Pec line, located between the two orogens and considered as a Mesozoic transform fault on the basis of geological observations, is the place where the torsion between the Dinarides and the Albanides recently occurred. On a local scale, four sites (out of 10) from two ridges located in northern Albania, south of the Scutari-Pec line but with a Dinaric trend, show that these two structures have undergone a -30 ø post-Eocene clockwise rotation. This intermediate value of rotation between the north and the south suggests that the Scutari-Pec line is, in fact, a rather wide transversal zone in which the two ridges are located. It acted as a decoupling zone between the Dinarides and the Albano-Hellenides during the Cenozoic and probably until the Pleistocene time. Introduction It is now well-established that the geometry of the Mediterranean Alpine belt arises from the Upper Cretaceous- Cenozoic collision between the African and European plates [Tapponnier, 1977; Dercourt et al., 1986]. Kinematic reconstructions show that the collision is presently taking place at an average rate of roughly 1 cm/yr [Argus et al., 1989]. Yet in many domains, deformation rates greater by almost an order of magnitude have been documented [Le Pichon et al., 1993]. These high rates result from changing regional trends of the chains, formation of arcs, and recent back arc oceanic basins, which regionally modify the overall pattern of the collision. In this framework, paleomagnetic studies which allow the description of rotation about vertical axis have proven crucial to unravel the complex tectonic pattern and to allow palinspastic reconstruction. It disappears about 20 km south of Dubrovnik where the Karst directly overthrusts the Dalmate zone (Figure 1). The sedimentary sequence of the Budva Zone remained entirely pelagic from Trias to upper Cretaceous. It became detritic during the uppermost Cretaceous (Maastrichtian) up to the Eocene when the flysch started to fill the preexisting basins. The Dalmate Zone (Kruja Zone in Albania) crops out in a narrow band all along the Adriatic coast and in all the eastern Adriatic islands (Figure 1). The Mesozoic sequence is entirely made of shelf limestones, very similar to the ones that outcrop in the Karst. For this reason the boundary between the Karst Zone and the Dalmate Zone is not clear in central and northern Dinarides. The calcareous sedimentation extends in the Dalmate Zone up to middle Eocene and is followed by middle- upper Eocene flysch. At the Eocene-Oligocene boundary the deformation reached the Dalmate Zone, which was divided in several tectonic units overthrusted onto the Adriatic foreland. Remaining samples were thermally demagnetized at 10 to 15 steps from room temperature up to the limit of reproducible results (320øC to 560øC). Rock magnetic experiments, such as acquisition of isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM), alternating field demagnetization of the saturation IRM (SIRM) and thermal demagnetization analyses of three-component IRM [Lowrie, 1990] were performed on some representative samples. Structural domains characterized by different strike, regional strike-slip faults, and arcuate structures have now been recognized, suggesting that the mechanisms of block rotations played an important role in the tectonic evolution of the area. For all these reasons we decided to perform further paleomagnetic sampling. Sampling sites were selected in areas characterized by different orientation of the fold axes (from NW-SE in the Latium-Abruzzi platform to NE-SW in the southern Sabina area) and having different tectonic styles and deformation patterns. The sampled sequences range from upper Cretaceous to Messinian and represent the youngest sediments available for paleomagnetic studies in each structural domain. By sampling wide stratigraphic intervals in some particular structures (e.g., the Prenestini Mountains) we were able to obtain temporal control on the different rotations. Rock magnetic experiments, such as acquisition of isothermal remanent magnetization (IRM), alternating field demagnetization of the saturation IRM (SIRM) and thermal demagnetization analyses of three-component IRM [Lowrie, 1990] were performed on some representative samples. These analyses showed that the red samples from the Scaglia Formation are mainly characterized by low-coercivity minerals such as magnetite with a small amount of high- coercivity minerals such as hematite. These analyses showed that the red samples from the Scaglia Formation are mainly characterized by low-coercivity minerals such as magnetite with a small amount of high- coercivity minerals such as hematite. Rock magnetic experiments demonstrate that these formations are dominated by magnetite. The tectonic setting of this region is characterized by NNW-SSE to N-S local structures resulting from the activity of transpressive mechanisms which have been recognized along the major N-S tectonic elements [Mattei and Miccadei, 1991; Ghisetti and Vezzani, 1991 ]. Low-Field Anisotropy of Magnetic Susceptibility (AMS) Results In the past few years AMS data yielded very important results concerning the strain history of rocks, in particular very weak or undeformed sedimentary sequences for which no other methods could be applied [Lowrie, 1989]. Although the AMS studies cannot substitute the petrofabric analyses in the strain studies, a strong correlation between the magnetic fabric detected by AMS analyses and the tectonic elements has been largely proved all around the world [Kligfield et al., 1981; Borradaile, 1988]. We measured AMS for sites sampled for paleomagnetic analyses. Data were analyzed using both the maximum density orientation and the tensorial statistics of Jelinek [1978]. The magnetic fabric is described by an ellipsoid in which Kmax, Kint, and Kmin represent the maximum, intermediate, and minimum axes.
